Initial hormonal therapy is continued until disease progression or unaccept- able adverse effects occur at which point up to 2 further hormonal regimens may be tried. If these fail, or sympto- matic visceral disease develops, the patient is a candidate for chemotherapy. A number of drugs have some activity in chemotherapy of metastatic breast cancer. The taxanes, and in particular do- cetaxel (which is considered the reference drug in meta- static breast cancer42) are acknowledged to be effective,43 and anthracyclines (doxorubicin, epirubicin, and the relat- ed drug mitoxantrone) are also widely used, although a systematic review suggested that their benefits in terms of tumour response did not extend to improved survival.44 The benefits of platinum-based therapy have not been es- tablished.45 Capecitabine, gemcitabine, and vinorelbine are active agents.3 There is considerable uncertainty as to whether combina- tion regimens offer any substantial benefit over sequential use of single drugs.3,42,46 Although a systematic review of older regimens suggested benefit from combination chem- otherapy,46 and this is the usual standard of care where therapy has curative intent,42 some do not consider the ev- idence of benefit from combination therapy persuasive,3 and toxicity is likely to be increased. Nonetheless, estab- lished combination regimens, including CMF and various anthracycline- and taxane-based regimens are in use,3,8 along with newer combinations, such as gemcitabine plus paclitaxel, vinorelbine plus epirubicin, or paclitaxel plus bevacizumab.3 Ixabepilone with or without capecitabine, is another option.3,47 In patients with HER2-overexpress- ing tumours, trastuzumab may be added to chemothera- py:3 the combination is markedly more effective in this group than chemotherapy alone,42 although use with an- thracyclines may be problematic because of the increased risk of cardiotoxicity.3 Higher response rates
